The writer effectively uses sensory details—particularly in the third paragraph—to make the setting and characters feel tangible and real. The narrative stimulates the senses of touch, smell, sound, and sight through vivid descriptions such as the "mild, all too sweet air of this late summer morning" (*in der linden, allzu süßen Luft dieses Spätsommermorgens*), the physical sensation of Casanova gripping the hilt of his sword, his worn-out clothes and patched linens, the visual details of the "pockmarked mistress" (*blatternarbiger Geliebten*) and the "faded chestnut trees" (*abgeblühten Kastanienbäumen*), as well as the sounds of the drunken husband "snoring" (*schnarchend*) and the peasant cart "creaking on" (*weiterknarren*) through the "dust and haze of the country road" (*im Staub und Dunst der Landstraße*).
